title: API 580 Training in Seattle: RBI Exam Prep Online
description: Self-paced API 580 exam prep for Puget Sound RBI teams: Washington's DMR rule, consequence near the water and closed-book practice, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 580 Training in Seattle: Risk Based Inspection Exam Prep for Puget Sound Refinery RBI and Damage Mechanism Review Teams
html:
API 580 exam prep for RBI teams around Puget Sound

Damage mechanism work at Washington refineries is no longer only a matter of company policy. Since the state added a refinery-specific part to its process safety rule, every refinery on the Sound has to run damage mechanism reviews on a fixed timetable, and the people who sit on those reviews are the same inspectors, corrosion engineers and planners who build and maintain RBI programmes. This page is for them, and for API 510, 570 and 653 inspectors whose intervals now come out of a risk model.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Seattle. The API 580 course is self-paced and online, and an instructor answers questions as you work through API RP 580 and the RBI ideas around it. The American Petroleum Institute sets eligibility, administers the examination and issues the certification; API's programme page says the API 580 exam can be scheduled at an in-person test centre or through remote proctoring. Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider, and the course does not certify anyone.

Washington's damage mechanism review rule, read by an RBI candidate

The Department of Labor and Industries added Part B to chapter 296-67 WAC, the state's process safety management chapter, and the refinery rules took effect in late December 2024. WAC 296-67-347 covers damage mechanism reviews (DMRs), and its requirements read like the front end of an RBI study:

  • Team. The review is done by a team with expertise in engineering, equipment and pipe inspection, damage and failure mechanisms and the operation of the process, including one member who knows the DMR methodology being used.
  • Content. It assesses process flow diagrams, identifies all potential damage mechanisms, confirms that materials of construction are appropriate, identifies ways to prevent or mitigate damage, and reviews operating parameters that could accelerate or reduce it. It also looks at past experience: inspection history, industry experience and applicable standards.
  • Timing. At least half of the initial DMRs are due within three years of Part B's effective date and the rest within five; each DMR is revalidated at least every five years, and a DMR is needed before approving a major change that may introduce a damage mechanism.
  • Priority and use. The employer sets the order of reviews from operating and maintenance history, the process hazard analysis schedule and inspection records, and the DMR must be available to the team performing the PHA.

The rule does not mention API RP 571, API 580, API RP 581 or risk-based inspection, and it does not require a certification for team members. What it does is create a steady demand for people who can describe damage mechanisms precisely and connect them to inspection, which is the knowledge the API 580 examination tests.

From a damage mechanism review to an RBI model

A DMR answers one question for each piece of equipment: how can it deteriorate here? RP 580 turns that into risk by adding the rest of the calculation, and the exam expects you to know where each piece comes from.

  • Probability of failure starts from the mechanisms the DMR identified, their susceptibility and expected rates, and then reflects how much the inspection history actually tells you. Inspection effectiveness is the bridge: a method that cannot detect the mechanism, however often it is applied, does little to reduce uncertainty.
  • Consequence of failure comes from the fluid, the inventory, the operating conditions and what is nearby, which is why the PHA team and the RBI team need the same information.
  • The inspection plan follows from the risk: which items, which methods, what extent and when, with mitigation other than inspection where inspection cannot lower the risk enough.
  • Reassessment is triggered by new inspection data, changes in process or operation, and the passing of time. Washington's DMR-before-major-change requirement is a local version of the reassessment discipline RP 580 describes.

Integrity operating windows sit between the two. A DMR's list of operating parameters that accelerate damage is the raw material for IOW limits, and an excursion outside them is the kind of process change that should send an RBI team back to its assessment.

The data an RBI team on the Sound has to gather

Data collection is a knowledge area of its own on the API 580 paper, and Puget Sound refineries give it real texture. Marathon says its Anacortes plant runs Canadian crude, domestic crude from North Dakota and the Alaska North Slope, and international crudes; HF Sinclair says its Puget Sound refinery processes mixed sweet and sour Canadian crude and Alaska North Slope crude. A shifting crude slate changes sulfur and acid loads from one campaign to the next, so an RBI model built on a single design case soon drifts from reality. EIA's capacity survey also lists sulfur recovery at every Washington refinery, from 11 short tons a day at Tacoma to 350 at the HF Sinclair plant, a rough indicator of how much sour service each one handles. Process history, inspection records with known coverage and accurate materials data matter as much as the risk method chosen.

Consequence of failure on the water's edge

Every refinery on the Sound sits beside protected water, and Ecology's permit pages say where each one sends treated wastewater: the Strait of Georgia for Cherry Point and Ferndale, Fidalgo Bay for the two Anacortes plants and the Blair Waterway for Tacoma. For an RBI team that geography lands in the environmental part of the consequence assessment. A release from a dock line, a transfer line on a trestle or a tank near the shoreline can reach water quickly, and Ecology regulates the oil-handling side of these sites as Class 1 facilities under chapter 173-180 WAC, with rules on transfer pipelines and storage tanks.

Business consequence matters as well. bp describes Cherry Point as a leading supplier of jet fuel to the Seattle and Portland international airports, and EIA's capacity survey lists only five refineries in the state, so an unplanned outage on a key unit is felt across the region's fuel supply. RP 580 lets an owner include financial and supply consequences alongside safety and environmental ones; the exam tests whether you know which categories exist and how they combine, not a particular company's matrix.

Fixed rules that bound a Washington RBI plan

An RBI study can move many inspection dates, but not all of them. A Puget Sound candidate should know where the local rules leave room.

  • Pressure vessels. WAC 296-104-100 sets biennial internal and external inspections for corroding unfired vessels but lets vessels in an owner-user inspection programme follow API 510 intervals. The state's in-service rules do not mention risk-based inspection; API 510 is the document that says when an RBI assessment may justify an interval or an on-stream inspection, so confirm with L&I how your programme is accepted.
  • Terminal and refinery tanks. Ecology's WAC 173-180-330 requires Class 1 facility storage tanks to be maintained, repaired and inspected to API 653, unless the operator proposes an equivalent strategy that Ecology approves.
  • Breakout tanks. For tanks on the Olympic pipeline system, 49 CFR 195.432(b) applies API 653 but excludes its risk-based internal interval alternative. PHMSA proposed in June 2026 to remove that exclusion, with caps on the intervals; the proposal was not a final rule when this page was written.
  • Transfer pipelines. Under WAC 173-180-340, bare buried transfer lines need thickness and corrosion-rate checks at half the remaining life or every five years, whichever is sooner, whatever a risk ranking says.

A closed-book scenario: same probability, different consequence

Two eight-inch carbon steel lines at a north Sound refinery carry the same diesel at the same temperature. Line A runs between a hydrotreater and tankage inside the unit fence. Line B runs out along a trestle to the dock. Both show the same thinning rate, the same inspection history and the same assessed probability of failure.

  1. Which carries the higher risk? Line B. With equal probability, risk follows consequence, and a release over water adds an environmental consequence that the in-unit line does not have.
  2. Will inspecting Line B more often lower its consequence? No. Inspection improves knowledge of the damage state and so lowers probability, or at least its uncertainty. Consequence falls only through mitigation such as leak detection, faster isolation, smaller inventory or containment.
  3. The owner switches Line B to biodiesel. What should happen? A management of change review and an RBI reassessment, because a new fluid can change both the damage mechanisms and the consequence. Under Washington's rule a major change that may introduce a damage mechanism also needs a DMR first.
  4. Which DMR finding would most change Line B's probability? External corrosion at the trestle supports from marine exposure, a mechanism Line A barely sees, and one that thickness readings away from the supports would miss.

The real paper is multiple choice, but its distractors exploit the same confusions: inspection that is assumed to reduce consequence, risk treated as probability alone, and reassessment forgotten after a change.

Who sits API 580 around Seattle, and how they qualify

Holders of a current API 510, 570 or 653 certification qualify automatically. Everyone else needs education plus petrochemical industry experience gained in the last 10 years: one year with a bachelor's degree in engineering or technology, two with a two-year degree or certificate, three with a high school diploma and five or more with no formal education. Because the requirement is petrochemical experience rather than work for an inspection agency, API 580 suits Washington refinery engineers who will never sit an inspector paper: corrosion and materials specialists on DMR teams, reliability engineers, PSM coordinators and inspection planners who maintain the RBI database. API reviews each application; the course does not count as experience.

Preparing for a closed-book paper from Seattle

The API 580 examination has 90 multiple-choice questions, 80 of them scored, in 3.25 hours, with no reference material. Self-paced preparation fits around refinery work, and the instructor is most useful for the questions RP 580 answers indirectly, such as why a particular inspection counts as more effective than another. Three habits help:

  • Learn the vocabulary exactly. Probability, consequence, risk, risk target, inspection effectiveness and mitigation have precise meanings in RP 580, and distractors use near-synonyms.
  • Tie each concept to a review you know. If you have sat on a Washington DMR, map its outputs to the RP 580 elements; the connection makes the closed-book material stick.
  • Choose the delivery that suits you. Remote proctoring needs a quiet, compliant room and a reliable connection; Prometric lists test centres in and around Seattle for candidates who would rather travel.

Exam preparation, RBI studies and sponsorship

Passing API 580 shows knowledge of RP 580; it does not make a candidate an RBI analyst, and running an assessment on a real unit takes data, a qualified team and the owner's approval. Owners who need an assessment rather than training can see remote risk-based inspection studies. Refinery inspection groups, engineering contractors and terminal operators can enrol several API 580 candidates, alongside others preparing for API 510, 570 or 653. Fees are quoted on request, and every candidate files a separate application with API.

faq.q: Does Washington's damage mechanism review rule mention RBI or API 580?
faq.a: No. WAC 296-67-347 sets out who must be on the DMR team, what the review covers and when it is due and revalidated, but it does not name API RP 571, API 580, API RP 581 or risk-based inspection, and it does not require any certification. Refiners decide for themselves whether to build their DMRs into an RBI programme. In practice the two share most of their inputs, which is why API 580 knowledge helps a DMR team member.

faq.q: Should I take API 580 at a Seattle-area test centre or by remote proctoring?
faq.a: API's API 580 page says the exam can be scheduled either way, so choose by circumstance. Remote proctoring saves the drive but needs a quiet room that meets the proctoring rules and a reliable connection for 3.25 hours. A Prometric centre removes the technology risk. Confirm the delivery options API offers when you apply, since API decides how the examination is delivered.

faq.q: Can an RBI assessment lengthen Washington's biennial vessel inspections?
faq.a: Possibly, through API 510 rather than the state rule itself. WAC 296-104-100 lets vessels in an owner-user inspection programme follow API 510 intervals instead of the biennial default, and API 510 describes when an RBI assessment may justify an interval or an on-stream inspection. The state rules do not mention RBI, so the owner should agree the approach with L&I. On the exam, focus on RP 580's principles rather than any state's rules.

faq.q: Are Olympic Pipeline breakout tanks allowed risk-based inspection intervals?
faq.a: Not under the current federal rule. 49 CFR 195.432(b) requires breakout tanks to be inspected under API 653 but excludes the code's risk-based alternative for setting internal inspection intervals. PHMSA proposed in June 2026 to lift that exclusion, with maximum intervals attached, but a proposal is not a rule; check the status before planning on it.

faq.q: Is environmental consequence tested on the API 580 exam?
faq.a: Consequence of failure is one of the ten knowledge areas in the Body of Knowledge, and RP 580 discusses the kinds of consequence an assessment weighs, from fire and toxic release to environmental and financial loss. Expect questions on what each category covers, how consequence combines with probability into risk and which actions reduce consequence as opposed to probability. You will not be asked to apply a Washington agency's rules, but understanding why a release near Puget Sound weighs heavily makes the principles easier to remember.

faq.q: I work at a pulp mill, not a refinery. Can I qualify for API 580?
faq.a: Unless you already hold a current API 510, 570 or 653 certification, API 580 eligibility rests on petrochemical industry experience, and API decides what counts. Mill experience may not meet that test on its own, so check with API before you apply. If you do hold one of the three inspector certifications from earlier refinery or terminal work, you qualify automatically.

faq.q: Will the course teach the RBI software my refinery uses?
faq.a: No. The course prepares you for the API 580 examination, which tests the concepts in RP 580 rather than any vendor's software. Knowing those concepts makes software output easier to question: why an item ranked where it did, what the inspection effectiveness assumption was, and what would trigger reassessment. Learn your site's tool from the site, and use the course to understand what it is doing.
